section_summaries.epidemiology: Trichinellosis is a zoonotic disease acquired by humans from eating insufficiently cooked infected meat. Nine Trichinella species infect wild and domestic animals globally, with humans being susceptible to clinical disease. Although declining in developed countries, outbreaks persist in developing regions, especially Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Africa. It is an important food-borne zoonosis, particularly from domestic swine (T. spiralis), though outbreaks from horsemeat and game animals also occur. Sylvatic and domestic ecological systems exist, with T. spiralis being highly infective to pigs. Prevention involves stringent barriers to wild animal exposure, proper cooking of meat to 160°F, and freezing meat (except for T. nativa).
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Humans acquire Trichinellosis by consuming raw or undercooked meat containing L1 Trichinella larvae. These larvae are freed by digestion in the stomach, resist gastric acid, and pass into the small intestine. They burrow into the columnar epithelium, undergo four molts, and develop into adult male and female worms, which then mate. Fertilized females discharge juvenile L1 newborn larvae for 4 to 16 weeks. These newborn larvae migrate to the lamina propria, enter the lymphatic or blood vessels, and are carried via arterial circulation to invade striated skeletal muscle cells. After invasion, they induce changes, culminating in a new cell phenotype termed the nurse cell, which in encapsulated Trichinella species is surrounded by a collagenous capsule. After 21 days, the larvae are fully infective and resistant to gastric juice. In humans, cyst calcification may begin within 6 months to a year, leading to the death of the encysted larvae.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: The degree of illness is usually proportional to the number of larvae ingested. Symptoms are divided into an early intestinal phase, a later muscle invasion phase associated with inflammatory and allergic responses, and a convalescent phase. The incubation period ranges from 5 to 51 days. The intestinal phase (first week) presents with gastrointestinal symptoms, low-grade fever, headache, dizziness, and weakness. The muscle invasion (parenteral) phase, starting 9-10 days after exposure, involves myositis with neutrophils, eosinophils, lymphocytes, and macrophages, leading to enlarged and edematous muscle fibers, especially in extraocular, masseter, laryngeal, tongue, diaphragm, neck, intercostal, and muscular attachments to tendons and joints. Symptoms include fever (up to 104°F), myalgia, periorbital/facial edema, eosinophilia, muscle swelling/tenderness, urticaria, splinter hemorrhages, and conjunctivitis. Severe cases can involve dyspnea, myocarditis (sometimes fatal), and neurologic complications such as intracerebral hemorrhage, meningitis, dizziness, ataxia, hysteria, psychotic disturbances, seizures, monoparesis, or coma. In the convalescent phase (second month), myalgia and fever decrease, but congestive heart failure may appear. Larvae remain alive in cysts for years, releasing antigens that maintain eosinophilia and antibody response. Fatal outcomes are infrequent, usually in massive infections, associated with myocarditis, encephalitis, or pneumonitis.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on clinical signs, history of raw or undercooked meat consumption, and specific laboratory findings. An algorithm can aid in identifying cases. Direct diagnosis involves muscle biopsy of superficial skeletal muscle (preferably deltoid or gastrocnemius), with a 1 cm³ specimen examined histologically, by compression, or by digestion in pepsin and hydrochloric acid to identify worms and species. A negative biopsy does not exclude light infections. Indirect diagnosis detects circulating antibodies 2-4 weeks post-infection using fluorescent antibody tests or ELISA with larval E/S antigen, confirmed by Western blot for TSL-1 antigen. Characteristic laboratory findings include eosinophilia, leukocytosis, elevated muscle enzymes, and increased immunoglobulin levels, especially total IgE. Differential diagnosis includes influenza or other viral fevers, distinguished by the history of meat ingestion, febrile myalgia, periorbital edema, and rising eosinophilia.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for trichinellosis has uncertainties due to limited controlled clinical trials. Symptomatic management includes analgesics, antipyretics, bed rest, and corticosteroids (prednisolone at 50 mg/day), especially for severe infections to prevent shock-like symptoms. Antiparasitic treatment involves oral albendazole (400 mg twice daily for 10-15 days) or mebendazole (200-400 mg three times daily for 3 days, then 400-500 mg three times daily for 10 days). Factors influencing treatment include Trichinella species, worm burden, duration of symptoms, and host immunocompetence. The use of albendazole or mebendazole in young children and pregnant women must be balanced against the risk of disease progression without therapy.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention of trichinellosis is achieved by stringent barriers in commercial and backyard pig production to avoid exposure to wild animals, especially commensal rats and uncooked meat scraps. Cooking meat to 160°F (71°C) is sufficient to kill larvae, and freezing meat is also effective for protecting consumers, except for Trichinella nativa which is freeze-resistant.

Muscular pain, facial edema, fever, chills, tachycardia, coma, respiratory difficulties, eosinophilia
Mental apathy, neurotoxic symptoms, possible myocarditis, anemia, muscular swelling

tables.title: Signs and Symptoms Useful in Assessing the Probability of Being Infected With Trichinella
rows: Positive serology (using a highly specific test)
Very unlikely: one A or one B or one C
Suspected: one A or two B and one C
Probable: three A and one C
Highly probable: three A and two C
Confirmed: three A, two C, and one D; any of groups A or B and one C and one D
